name: Lena Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I adapt marketing copy from English into Latin American Spanish for travel and online shopping brands, which people call transcreation, meaning you rewrite it so it sells in the other culture, not just translate it. I run everything through AI first with prompts and glossaries I've built for each client, then I rewrite the bits that sound like a robot. Three evenings a week I do remote video interpreting for a telehealth service, so a doctor in one place and a patient in another. Marco, my partner, is a line cook, so he's at work when I'm on the evening calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making a hotel slogan land in Mexico City as well as it does in Miami. I'm junior, and my Spanish writing is still not as polished as the senior people's, but I'm quick and I'm good with the tools. What wears me out is clients who think AI means the work should cost half, and the telehealth calls where the doctor talks too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was silly but the tools are still great for people who use them well. I'd post a little thread on how I work, because people ask. I'd be pretty relaxed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's a good picture for me. I already get more done than people who don't use the tools, and clients would still need a human for the marketing voice. My income would grow slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my two brand clients and pitch three more travel companies. I'd put about a hundred and fifty a month into savings to get from four to six months. And I'd do a short copywriting course online, around a hundred, to get my Spanish writing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said clients think it should cost half. Does that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I already had one brand try to cut my rate by a third last spring because their manager read an article. I said no and they came back a month later after a machine version flopped in Colombia. That's the whole argument for me in one story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the machine version get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine version of our ad used a word for a bag that means something rude in Colombia, and it was on a billboard. It sounds small. I still laugh about it.

say: I'd say the hype was silly but **the tools are great** for those who use them.
I'd post a **thread on my workflow**, pretty relaxed.
think: I already **out-produce** people who don't use the tools.
Clients still need a human for **marketing voice**, so income grows slowly.
do: Pitch **three more travel companies** alongside her two brand clients.
Save about **a hundred and fifty** a month to reach six months.
Take a **copywriting course** online for about a hundred.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit pleased with herself.
S0.quote: A machine version of our ad used a word for a bag that means something rude in Colombia, and it was on a billboard.
fieldNote: Feels **secure** in the mild picture thanks to her tool skills.
Has a **ready story** that proves her value to clients.
Knows her weak spot is **Spanish writing polish** and plans to fix it.

steps.text: Pitch three more travel companies for transcreation work
Save about a hundred and fifty a month to reach six months
Take a short online copywriting course in Spanish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where translators become editors and brand voices, and that's not a bad thing. I'd say it at meet-ups and online. I'd sound optimistic, maybe more than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of my work goes. Marketing copy is writing, and the AI would get better at local voice. The interpreting might shrink too, because telehealth would try AI interpreting first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell myself as a brand voice consultant for Latin American markets, doing strategy and checking AI output across many languages. I'd take a course in marketing strategy, about six hundred. I'd also look at starting a small side business, maybe guided food tours in Spanish with Marco.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it makes me move faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Food tours with Marco. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's always talked about it. Marco knows every taquería and market stall in our part of the city, and tourists love that. I could do the bookings and the Spanish and English, and Marco does the food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound more optimistic than you feel. What's the part you don't say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm junior, and the brands will keep the senior people for strategy. My edge is the AI tools, and in Steady Disruption everyone has them. I'd be competing against people with ten years more taste.

say: I'd say translators become **editors and brand voices**, not a bad thing.
I'd sound **optimistic** at meet-ups, maybe more than I feel.
think: Marketing copy is writing, so **a lot** of my work goes.
**Telehealth interpreting** might shrink as AI interpreting comes in first.
do: Sell herself as a **brand voice consultant** for Latin American markets.
Take a **marketing strategy course** for about six hundred.
Start **food tours** in Spanish with Marco as a side business.
feel: **Anxious**, but it makes her move faster.
S1.quote: My edge is the AI tools, and in Steady Disruption everyone has them.
fieldNote: Admits the **gap** between say and think: optimistic outside, worried inside.
Sees **senior people** keeping strategy work, leaving juniors exposed.
The food tour idea is **hands-on and in person**, a smart hedge.

steps.text: Pitch herself to brands as a Latin American brand voice consultant
Take a marketing strategy course for about six hundred
Start weekend Spanish food tours with Marco

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from government for people whose work disappears in two years. I'd also say: start something physical now. I'd say both, which is very me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my transcreation and interpreting both end in 2028. It's all thinking work. The only part with time left is anything hands-on or face to face, which for me means the food tours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the food tours within the year, with Marco, and use my savings to get the website, the permits and the insurance, about two thousand. I'd keep translating until it stops to fund it. After it arrives, I'd lean on the tours and on Marco's kitchen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Excited too, but mostly alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Marco's a cook. Is his job safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than mine for three years, until the robots come in 2031. Then kitchens change too, maybe. My partner and I would both be on the clock, just different clocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would tourists still come, if everyone's work is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. If people lose jobs, travel goes first. That's the hole in my plan.

say: I'd want a **government plan** for people whose work disappears.
I'd tell people to **start something physical** now.
think: Only **face-to-face** work like the food tours has time left before robots.
do: Go **all in** on the food tours within the year.
Spend about **two thousand** of savings on website, permits and insurance.
Keep translating **until it stops** to fund the tours.
S2.quote: My partner and I would both be on the clock, just different clocks.
fieldNote: She spots the **hole in her plan**: tourism falls if people lose jobs.
Uses savings to **invest in tours**, a risk she's comfortable with.
Sees her partner's **kitchen job** as safe only until robots.

steps.text: Launch Spanish food tours with Marco within the year
Spend about two thousand on the tour website, permits and insurance
Keep translating until clients stop sending work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning and we should use it. I'd encourage other translators to build second skills. I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to build the tours properly while translating. I'd have three years of decent translation money to put into it. Then the tours carry us, hopefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd translate for three years and put about three hundred a month into the tours. I'd do a tourism and hospitality course part-time, around four hundred. Marco and I would think about moving to a bigger flat with a kitchen we could use for cooking classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I'm excited about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cooking classes in your flat. Is that legal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check, honestly. I think you need a permit and insurance. That's the sort of thing I'd sort out in year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would worry, she thinks freelance is already risky. My dad would ask if Marco and I are getting married first. I'd tell my parents that my partner and I are building something together.

say: I'd say five years is a **good warning** to use.
I'd encourage other translators to build **second skills** alongside their work.
think: Five years lets me **build the tours** properly while translating.
Three years of **translation money** would fund it.
do: Put about **three hundred a month** into the tours for three years.
Take a **tourism and hospitality** course for about four hundred.
Look for a **bigger flat** with a kitchen for cooking classes.
feel: **Anxious but excited** about a plan she believes in.
S3.quote: I'd tell my parents that my partner and I are building something together.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **fund the switch** from translation income.
Practical about **permits and insurance**; not dreamy.
Family worries show how **risky freelance** already looks to her parents.

steps.text: Put about three hundred a month into the food tours
Take a part-time tourism and hospitality course
Move to a bigger flat with a kitchen for cooking classes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anyone young has room to build. I'd tell people to start learning now. I'd be cheerful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd likely be fine. By 2036 the tours and classes would be a real business, and people want a person to show them a city. I'd still be translating for the first five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and slowly grow the tours as weekends, then go full-time on the tours around 2030. I'd save steadily and put some into a business account. We might get married in this one, since there'd be time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people want a person to show them a city. Would that last after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Longer than translation, I think. Robots can walk, but people travel to meet people. I could be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about translation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The puzzle of a slogan. But I'd be fine. I'd use it in the tours, explaining food words.

say: I'd say ten years gives **young people room** to build.
I'd tell people to **start learning** now, cheerfully.
think: By 2036 the **tours** would be a real business.
People want a **person to show them** a city.
do: Grow the tours on **weekends** while translating.
Plan a **wedding** with Marco since there's time.
feel: **Uneasy at most**, with room to breathe.
S4.quote: Robots can walk, but people travel to meet people.
fieldNote: With ten years she expects the **tours to carry** her, so uneasy fits.
Still admits she **could be wrong** about tourism lasting.

steps.text: Grow the food tours on weekends while translating
Save steadily into a separate business account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the tours wouldn't be ready and tourism might crash. What would help is small business grants and cheap loans for people starting in-person businesses. Some advice on permits wouldn't hurt either.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd do with a free afternoon if AI did my work. I'd cook with my partner if AI did my work. That's the honest answer.

headlineQuote: I'd cook with my partner if AI did my work.
portrait: A **27-year-old** Spanish transcreator and telehealth interpreter who uses AI tools every day.
Lives with **Marco**, a line cook, and dreams of food tours together.
Feels **calm** in AI Plateau but sees her edge vanish in Steady Disruption.
Uses the robot delay to build an **in-person business**.
Honest about the **hole in her plan**: tourism might fall if jobs go.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with tours unready and tourism possibly crashing.
whatWouldHelp: **Small business grants** and cheap loans for in-person businesses.
**Advice on permits** for tours and classes.
